core_idea: Model each pile only by the exponent of 2 dividing it, then classify positions by the minimum such exponent. Odd minimum gives the first player a move to a losing even state; even minimum with all piles tied is losing for the first player; even minimum with a larger pile present can be perpetually maintained as a draw.
key_observations: A move is possible exactly when some pile has positive 2-adic valuation, and the game ends when all valuations are 0.
When all piles have the same valuation c > 0, any move decreases every pile's valuation to c - 1.
If a pile with the current minimum valuation is chosen, all piles can collapse to that minimum-minus-one level.
The parity of the minimum valuation determines whether collapsing the game hands the opponent a winning or losing synchronized state.
When the minimum valuation is even but not shared by all piles, choosing a pile above the minimum preserves both a minimum pile and a higher-valued pile, so neither player is forced to end the game.
Counting configurations can be done by fixing the exact minimum valuation, and counting all-equal valuation cases separately.
reasoning_patterns: Replace large numeric state with the invariant-relevant valuation or rank.
Classify game states by a small aggregate statistic, such as the minimum, instead of the full configuration.
Analyze special synchronized states first because transitions become simple and reveal winning/losing parity.
Use a move that collapses the state to a controlled canonical form.
For draw games, identify a cycle or maintained invariant that both players can use to avoid losing.
Count objects by exact minimum using difference of nested counts.
Separate terminal/winning/losing/drawing classes, then count the remainder by complement.
questions: What part of each number actually affects legal moves and transitions?
Is there an invariant or monotone statistic that controls the outcome?
What happens when all components have the same key value?
Can I move to a canonical state whose outcome is already known?
Does the parity of a depth, valuation, or distance decide the winner?
If winning is impossible, can both players preserve a non-terminal condition forever?
Can I count configurations by fixing the exact minimum?
Which cases are easier to count directly, and which can be obtained by complement?
